questions.title: What is the scope of presidential authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) after Trump v. Hawaii?
questions.question_body: The court cites Trump v. Hawaii for the proposition that § 1182(f) 'exudes deference' to the President and that courts cannot engage in 'a searching inquiry into the persuasiveness of the President's justifications.' But this seems to give the President nearly unlimited power to suspend entry of any class of aliens. Are there any meaningful limits on this authority? The statute says the President must find that entry 'would be detrimental to the interests of the United States' - is this a substantive requirement or purely procedural? Can courts ever invalidate a suspension under § 1182(f), or is the President's determination effectively unreviewable?

questions.title: How do courts determine whether a statute creates a mandatory duty or merely authorizes discretionary action?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling to understand the dispute between the majority and Judge Lee about 8 U.S.C. § 1522. The majority points to the word 'shall' in various subsections to argue that the statute mandates providing refugee services. But Judge Lee counters that the statute's title uses 'Authorization' and that the funding provisions say the Director 'is authorized' to provide assistance. How do courts typically resolve this kind of tension? When a statute's title says 'authorization' but the substantive provisions use 'shall,' which controls? Are there canons of statutory construction that apply here?

questions.title: What does 'to the extent of available appropriations' mean in federal benefit statutes?
questions.question_body: Section 1522(a)(1)(A) says the Director shall provide certain services 'to the extent of available appropriations.' The majority seems to read this as creating a mandatory obligation so long as Congress has appropriated funds. But could the executive branch argue that even with appropriations, the language gives them discretion over whether services are 'available'? And does the fact that Congress appropriated money (though reduced by the Rescissions Act) mean the 'available appropriations' condition is satisfied, or can the executive still decline to spend appropriated funds?

questions.title: Can the President suspend refugee admissions but still be required to serve refugees already admitted?
questions.question_body: The court reaches different conclusions on different parts of the case: the government is likely to prevail on the admissions suspension under § 1182(f), but unlikely to prevail on the services claim under § 1522. I'm confused about the relationship between these two issues. If the President can suspend refugee admissions entirely, why would Congress have required services for refugees who are already here? And does the court's ruling mean that the executive order is partially valid and partially invalid, or is the services requirement a separate statutory obligation that exists regardless of the admissions suspension?

questions.title: What standard do courts use when deciding whether to grant a stay pending appeal?
questions.question_body: The court applies the four-factor test from Nken v. Holder but says the first two factors (likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable injury) are 'the most critical.' What does this mean in practice? Does a strong showing on likelihood of success essentially decide the stay question, or can a party still lose a stay even if they're likely to succeed on the merits? Also, how does the stay standard differ from the standard for granting a preliminary injunction in the first place?

questions.title: What is the legal status of 'conditionally approved' refugees in the admission process?
questions.question_body: The earlier stay order created a carveout for individuals who were 'conditionally approved for refugee status' before January 20, 2025. What exactly does 'conditional approval' mean in the refugee context? Does this create some kind of procedural due process interest or expectation that the government must complete processing? And why would the motions panel treat conditionally approved refugees differently from those who had merely applied - is there a legal significance to the conditional approval status?

questions.title: What APA violations are alleged when the government terminates cooperative agreements?
questions.question_body: The court says the government is unlikely to prevail on at least one of plaintiffs' APA challenges, but doesn't explain the exact violations. When the State Department terminated all the cooperative agreements with resettlement organizations, what APA procedures would have been required? Is this about rulemaking vs. adjudication, or about arbitrary and capricious review under § 706? And what's the remedy if the termination was procedurally deficient - can the court order the government to reinstate the agreements, or just to follow proper procedures going forward?

questions.title: Can a court order the executive branch to reinstate terminated contracts or cooperative agreements?
questions.question_body: The court directs the government to 'reinstate such cooperative agreements necessary to provide reception and placement services.' But these are contracts with private nonprofit organizations that the government terminated. Can a court really order the government to enter back into contracts with specific private parties? What if the organizations don't want to resume the agreements, or if the government has legitimate concerns about their performance? And what's the difference between a 'cooperative agreement' and a regular contract for purposes of judicial review of termination?
